hints: Recall how s orbitals are spherical and p orbitals are dumbbell shaped with two lobes, then think how many lobes a typical d orbital shows.
walkthrough:
Picture the orbital family**
Think beside me: $s$ is a sphere, $p$ is a dumbbell with 2 lobes. Most $d$ orbitals go one step further and have 4 lobes arranged like a four leaf clover, all meeting at the nucleus. That is all you need to draw.

Draw an accepted shape**
Draw four touching lobes in one plane, e.g. $d_{xy}$ or $d_{x^2-y^2}$, with axes if you like. The $d_{z^2}$ shape with two lobes along z plus a doughnut ring around the centre is also accepted.
Final answer: Sketch showing a d-orbital, e.g. four lobes arranged in a clover leaf shape (or $d_{z^2}$ with two lobes plus central torus).

hints: Think about why Zn and Sc are often excluded: focus on the ions they form, not just the atom, and which subshell must be incomplete.
walkthrough:
Use the ion, not the atom**
A common slip is to say an element with a partially filled d orbital. That would wrongly include Sc and Zn. Cambridge defines it by what the element can do as an ion.

Give the precise definition**
A transition element forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d subshell. For example, $Fe^{2+}$ is $3d^6$ and $Cu^{2+}$ is $3d^9$, both incomplete, whereas $Zn^{2+}$ is $3d^{10}$ full and so Zn is not a transition element.
Final answer: An element that forms one or more stable ions with a partially filled / incomplete d subshell.

hints: Recall who supplies both electrons when a ligand with a lone pair attaches to a vacant orbital on the central metal ion.
walkthrough:
See the electron donation**
Picture a ligand like $:NH_3$ or $:Cl^-$ with a lone pair moving into an empty orbital on the metal ion. Only the ligand supplies both shared electrons.

Name the bond**
When both bonding electrons come from one atom, we call it a dative covalent bond, also called a coordinate bond.
Final answer: Dative covalent / coordinate bonding.

hints: Use oxygen as -2 and balance total charge to zero to work out the two common oxidation states of iron in its simple oxides.
walkthrough:
Apply the oxygen rule**
Take oxide $O$ as -2. For a neutral oxide the iron oxidation numbers must cancel the oxygen total.

Write both oxides**
In $\text{FeO}$, $+2 -2 = 0$ so Fe is +2. In $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$, $2 \times (+3) + 3 \times (-2) = 0$ so Fe is +3.
Final answer: $\text{FeO}$, Fe oxidation number +2 and $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$, Fe oxidation number +3.

hints: Remember co-ordination number counts bonded ligands, and for monodentate ligands it equals the number of ligands in the formula.
Calculate complex charge by adding metal ion charge to total ligand charge ($\text{CO}$ is neutral, $\text{CN}^-$ is -1).
walkthrough:
Complete the nickel row**
Co-ordination number is 4 and $\text{CO}$ is monodentate, so 4 $\text{CO}$ ligands bind: $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$. $\text{CO}$ is neutral, so charge = $+2 + 4(0) = 2+$. Hence $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]^{2+}$.

Complete the iron row**
Overall charge is 3-. Let n be number of $\text{CN}^-$: $+3 + n(-1) = -3$, so $n = 6$. With monodentate $\text{CN}^-$, co-ordination number = 6 and formula is $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$.
Final answer: For $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ / $\text{CO}$ / 4: formula $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]^{2+}$, charge 2+. For $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ / $\text{CN}^-$ / 3-: co-ordination number 6, formula $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$.

hints: Think of the isomerism where identical ligands can be next to each other or opposite each other in octahedral and square planar complexes.
walkthrough:
Spot the same pattern**
Both $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{2+}$ (octahedral) and $\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2$ (square planar) have formula type $MA_4B_2$. The two B ligands can be adjacent or opposite.

Name it**
Different spatial arrangement with the same connectivity is stereoisomerism of the cis-trans type, also called geometric isomerism.
Final answer: Cis-trans / geometric isomerism.

hints: For the octahedral Cu complex, place the two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands at 90 degrees for cis and at 180 degrees for trans.
For the square planar Pt complex, place the two $\text{NH}_3$ (or two Cl) adjacent for cis and opposite for trans.
walkthrough:
Draw the octahedral pair**
For $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{2+}$, keep Cu in the centre with six positions. In the cis isomer put the two $\text{NH}_3$ groups on adjacent corners, 90 degrees apart, e.g. one up and one to the side, with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in the other four sites. In the trans isomer put the two $\text{NH}_3$ groups opposite, 180 degrees apart, e.g. top and bottom.

Draw the square planar pair**
For $\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2$, keep Pt in the centre with four planar positions. In the cis isomer put the two $\text{NH}_3$ next to each other (and the two Cl next to each other). In the trans isomer put the two $\text{NH}_3$ opposite each other (and the two Cl opposite each other).

Final answer: One cis-trans pair for $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{2+}$: cis has $2 \times \text{NH}_3$ at 90 degrees, trans has $2 \times \text{NH}_3$ at 180 degrees. One cis-trans pair for $\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2$: cis has $2 \times \text{NH}_3$ adjacent (90 degrees), trans has $2 \times \text{NH}_3$ opposite (180 degrees).

hints: Write $K_{stab}$ as products over reactants, omitting $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ because it is a pure liquid.
Deduce units by putting concentration units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ into the expression and cancelling.
walkthrough:
Write the expression**
For equilibrium 5: $$[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{NH}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$ $K_{stab}$ includes aqueous species only, so: $$K_{stab} = \frac{[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{NH}_3)_2^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^2}$$ Note the squared $\text{NH}_3$ term for 2 moles.

Work out the units**
Put units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ in: $$\text{units} = \frac{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2} = \frac{1}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^2} = \text{dm}^{6} \text{mol}^{-2}$$
Final answer: $K_{stab} = \frac{[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{NH}_3)_2^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^2}$ units = $\text{dm}^{6} \text{mol}^{-2}$.

hints: Count aqueous particles on each side (ignore $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ for disorder comparison or count all species) and link more product particles to greater disorder.
walkthrough:
Count the particles**
Look at disorder. In equilibrium 4: $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + en \rightarrow [\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(en)]^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, that is 2 particles to 3 particles, a net gain. In equilibrium 5: $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + 2\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, that is 3 particles to 3 particles, no net gain.

Link to entropy**
More independent particles means more ways of distributing energy, so greater disorder. Hence $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is positive (+23 $\text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$) for 4 but slightly negative for 5.

Final answer: Equilibrium 4 has a net increase in moles: 2 moles reactants to 3 moles products, whereas equilibrium 5 has the same number of moles on both sides, 3 to 3, so $\Delta S$ is more positive for 4.

hints: Recall larger $K_{stab}$ means the equilibrium lies further to the right and the product complex is more stable relative to the aqua complex.
walkthrough:
Compare the constants**
The three copper complexes are $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(en)]^{2+}$ and $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{NH}_3)_2]^{2+}$. $K_{stab}$ for formation of the en complex (equilibrium 4) is $3.98 \times 10^{10}$, much larger than $5.01 \times 10^{7}$ for the ammonia complex.

Choose the most stable**
A larger $K_{stab}$ means a more stable product. So $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(en)]^{2+}$ is the most stable, consistent with the bidentate chelate effect.
Final answer: Copper complex $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4(en)]^{2+}$ because it has the largest / highest $K_{stab}$ ($3.98 \times 10^{10}$ > $5.01 \times 10^{7}$).
